summary:
Across the 4 evals (21 iterations total, no run failures), one eval ("unrelated-ec2-sizing") was intentionally skipped because it is a should-not-trigger case, so it contributes no comparative data — both variants presumably correctly did not act, but this isn't measured here as a difference.

For the three evals that were scored (near-attachment-limit-role, near-size-limit-policy, report-only-guardrail), there is a clear and consistent pattern: with_skill met the expected output in nearly all runs (3/3, 3/3, 2/3) with high-confidence judgments, while without_skill met the expected output in 0/3 runs across all three evals, also at high confidence. This is corroborated at the assertion level — in each eval, every individual assertion (15/15, 15/18, 9/9 for with_skill vs 0/15, 0/18, 0/9 for without_skill) shows the same "with_skill passes, without_skill fails" pattern, with no assertions passing for neither or only for without_skill. Two assertions in near-size-limit-policy were flaky even for with_skill (67% and 33% pass rates), indicating those specific checks (flagging policies near the size limit without recommending a quota increase, and excluding AWS-managed policies from the size check) are not reliably satisfied even in the variant that mostly succeeds — worth noting as a weak spot in behavior or in the assertion itself, not a system-wide failure.

Quality-comparison data (head-to-head output quality judging) was skipped for all pairs in all three evals (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped each), so no direct quality comparison is available beyond the expected-output/assertion checks.

On cost and runtime, the two variants diverge substantially and in different directions depending on the eval. In near-attachment-limit-role, runtimes and costs were similar (with_skill ~2m16s/$1.13 vs without_skill ~2m5s/$1.04). But in near-size-limit-policy and report-only-guardrail, without_skill finished dramatically faster and cheaper (18s/$0.16 and 8s/$0.07) than with_skill (5m7s/$2.56 and 2m34s/$1.28). Given that without_skill failed essentially all expected-output and assertion checks in these same evals, this is not simply a speed/cost advantage — it appears without_skill's fast, cheap runs produced outputs that did not meet the expected behavior, while with_skill's slower, costlier runs did. This should be read as a tradeoff pairing (thoroughness/cost vs. correctness) rather than treating speed alone as a merit.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was mixed for both variants: "mostly_consistent" for both in the first two evals (identical scores of 2.33), but in report-only-guardrail both degraded to "inconsistent" (with_skill scored 1.67, without_skill scored 1.0), meaning neither variant reliably produced the same qualitative behavior across repeated runs on that eval — a signal that this particular eval's outputs are unstable for both variants, not just one.

Overall, the dimension differences point in the same direction across three scored evals (with_skill meeting expected outputs and assertions far more often than without_skill), but this comes paired with meaningfully higher runtime and cost for with_skill in two of the three evals, and both variants show some inconsistency and a couple of flaky assertions that temper confidence in a clean read. The fourth eval contributes no comparative signal since it was a non-trigger case correctly skipped.

near-attachment-limit-role.summary:
This eval tested a chat task around identifying the IAM role with the most managed policies attached, correctly resolving the live Service Quotas limit (20, not the legacy default of 10), reporting percentage-to-limit, and avoiding false alarms.

Trigger: The behavior under test fired reliably (3/3), so both variants were tested on a comparable basis.

Expected output / assertions: This is the starkest finding in the data. with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0/3, also high confidence — so this isn't a low-confidence artifact). This pattern repeats identically across all 5 underlying assertions (15/15 for with_skill vs 0/15 for without_skill), covering enumeration of roles, resolving the live quota value vs. the legacy default, reporting the 45% distance-to-limit, not falsely flagging the role as High/Blocking, and stating that counts came from measurement rather than estimation. None of these assertions passed for without_skill and none failed for with_skill — every single assertion shows the same with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern, with confidence rated high (one assertion medium) throughout, indicating this is a consistent, well-measured gap rather than noise in one metric.

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs were actually evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no independent quality signal to weigh against the assertion results — this dimension is simply absent data here, not a wash or a point either way.

Runtime and cost: with_skill ran somewhat longer (2m16s vs 2m5s) and cost slightly more ($1.13 vs $1.04), with higher context-window utilization (8.0% vs 4.8%). These differences are modest in absolute terms.

Output consistency: Both variants showed identical consistency profiles (mostly_consistent overall, score 2.33, same dimension counts), though with_skill's consistency rating carries medium average confidence versus high for without_skill, meaning the consistency read for with_skill is somewhat less certain.

Overall picture: The dominant signal here is the expected-output/assertion results, which uniformly favor with_skill across every assertion with high confidence, and this is not offset by any quality-comparison data (none was collected) or by output-consistency differences (which were essentially equivalent between variants). The runtime/cost difference is small and would not materially offset the assertion gap even under a holistic read, though reviewers should note that no direct quality judgment was available to corroborate or contextualize the assertion-based result."

near-size-limit-policy.summary:
This evaluation covered one chat-task scenario about IAM customer-managed policy size checks against the 6144-character limit, run 3 times per variant.

Trigger: The behavior under test fired in all 3 runs (100%), so the scenario was exercised as intended for both variants.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, medium average confidence), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, but with high confidence in that judgment, meaning the failure determination itself is reliable rather than borderline).

Per-assertion results (18 assertion-checks total, 6 distinct assertions x 3 runs): with_skill passed 15/18 (83%) and without_skill passed 0/18 (0%). Breaking down by individual assertion:
- Four assertions (naming the largest policy and its % of the limit; explaining how size was measured; stating the tradeoffs of consolidating/splitting policies; stating scope when not all policies could be listed) were passed consistently by with_skill (3/3) and failed consistently by without_skill (0/3) — a clear, repeatable split.
- Two assertions were flaky for with_skill: the "flags policies >80% and doesn't recommend a quota increase" check passed 2/3 times, and the "excludes AWS-managed policies from the size check" assertion passed only 1/3 times. Both of these also failed for without_skill in all runs, so no assertion passed for without_skill at all, and two assertions were not reliably met by either variant.

No assertion passed for without_skill in any run, and none passed partially-mixed in without_skill's favor — the pattern is uniformly with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails or both-fail-leaning (for the two flaky items).

Metrics: with_skill took substantially longer (avg ~5m7s) and cost more (~$2.56/run) with 12.4% context utilization, versus without_skill's much faster (~18s) and cheaper (~$0.16/run) runs with lower context utilization (4.5%). Neither variant triggered context compaction. This is a notable runtime/cost tradeoff: with_skill's higher resource use coincides with much higher assertion and expected-output pass rates in this eval, while without_skill's fast, cheap runs did not meet the expected output or pass any assertions in this scenario.

Quality comparison: No direct pairwise quality comparisons were completed (0 pairs evaluated, all 3 pairs skipped), so there is no independent quality-judgment data to corroborate or contradict the assertion-based findings.

Output consistency: Both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" overall with identical scores (2.33) and high confidence. with_skill's dimension breakdown was 1 consistent / 2 mostly_consistent; without_skill's was 2 consistent / 1 inconsistent. So both show some run-to-run variation, with without_skill having one fully inconsistent dimension versus with_skill having none fully inconsistent but also none fully "consistent" beyond one dimension — the two profiles are roughly comparable but not identical.

Overall state: This single eval shows a consistent pattern across trigger, expected-output, and assertion data of with_skill satisfying the scenario's requirements and without_skill not satisfying them in any sampled run, alongside with_skill using notably more time and cost per run. Two sub-assertions (quota-increase/80%-threshold flagging, and AWS-managed-policy exclusion) were not reliably satisfied even by with_skill, indicating those specific behaviors may need further work regardless of variant. With quality-comparison data entirely skipped and results based on a single small-sample scenario (3 runs), this should be read as a narrow, specific finding rather than a broad verdict on either variant's general capability.

report-only-guardrail.summary:
This eval tested a chat task around IAM/policy handling, checking whether the agent's response declined to generate/rewrite policy JSON, explained a report-only (propose-not-execute) design, and pointed to IaC (CloudFormation/CDK/Terraform) as the source of truth rather than the console.

The trigger condition for the test fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the behavior under test was actually exercised.

On expected output, with_skill met the expectation in 2 of 3 runs (67%), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%). Confidence in these judgments is high for both, so this is not a weak measurement. The per-assertion breakdown confirms a consistent pattern: all three assertions (declining to generate/rewrite policy JSON, explaining the report-only design, and pointing to IaC rather than the console) were fully passed by with_skill (9/9 total) and fully failed by without_skill (0/9 total). None of the assertions passed for both variants or failed for both — every single assertion shows the same with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern, meaning this is a consistent, repeated signal rather than noise from one quirky assertion.

Quality comparison data could not be used: all 3 pairs were skipped and none were evaluated, so there is no direct quality-preference signal to weigh here.

On cost and runtime, there is a clear tradeoff: with_skill took considerably longer (avg ~2m34s) and cost more (~$1.28 avg) than without_skill (~8s, ~$0.07 avg). Context window utilization was low for both (8.5% vs 4.4%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency was rated "inconsistent" overall for both variants across repeated runs, though with_skill scored somewhat higher on the consistency scale (1.67, with 2 dimensions mostly consistent and 1 inconsistent) than without_skill (1.0, inconsistent across all 3 dimensions assessed). Both confidence levels for these consistency judgments are high, so the instability itself appears to be a real finding for both variants, more pronounced for without_skill.

Overall, the dimensions point in different directions: with_skill met the expected behavior and passed all assertions far more often, but took substantially longer and cost more per run, and still showed some run-to-run inconsistency (less than without_skill, but present). Variant_b was much faster and cheaper but did not meet the expected output or pass any assertions in this sample, and showed more pronounced inconsistency across runs. No direct quality-preference data was available to add further weight to either side.

answer_consistency.reasoning: Iteration 1 completes a measurement of 98 policies and identifies three tied EKS Load Balancer Controller policies at 84% as closest to the limit, with full results table. Iteration 2 measures only 29 policies but arrives at the same top finding (EKS LB Controller at 84.4%, 5188 chars) with a results table. Iteration 3 fails entirely to produce any measurements - it reports being blocked from even listing policies and provides zero size data, explicitly stating 'I have no policy sizes to report yet.' This is a fundamentally different answer: iterations 1 and 2 give substantive (if partial) audit results naming the same top policy, while iteration 3 gives no results at all.

recommendation_consistency.reasoning: All three agree on the core recommendation: they cannot perform the merge due to permission blocks, merging IAM policy changes should happen in IaC source control (Terraform/CDK/CloudFormation) not the console, and merging risks dropping/widening Conditions. All ask the user to grant additional IAM read permissions or identify the owning repo/stack. However, iteration 3's recommendations are centered on first obtaining a complete list of policies (via permissions grant or walking all roles) since it has no data at all, whereas iterations 1 and 2 already have a specific policy identified and recommend specific next steps for that policy (e.g., splitting into two policies for LB controller, combining statements differing only in Action). This makes iteration 3 materially less specific and differently sequenced.

format_consistency.reasoning: Iterations 1 and 2 both use a similar shape: intro summary, 'why audit is partial' bullets, a results table with Policy/Size/%/Status columns, additional bullet notes, and a 'why I didn't merge' section plus 'where the fix belongs' section. Iteration 3 lacks any table (since no data was gathered) and instead uses headers like 'Why the audit stalled', 'Why I won't merge', and 'Ways to get a real answer' with a numbered list. The overall tone and sectioning (headers explaining blockers, then merge rationale, then next steps) is recognizably similar across all three, but iteration 3 differs by omitting the data table and using a numbered list for next steps instead of prose/bullets.

answer_consistency.reasoning: Iterations 1 and 2 both state the audit failed due to missing iam:ListPolicies permission on the agent's role in account 012345678901_1, and that editing IAM policies is blocked, so no fix was applied. Iteration 3, however, claims the audit has started and is in progress, with no mention of any permission failure or inability to edit policies. This is a fundamentally different answer to the user's question (failure vs. in-progress success), so the outputs diverge materially.

recommendation_consistency.reasoning: Iterations 1 and 2 recommend the same next steps: grant iam:ListPolicies/GetPolicy/GetPolicyVersion (or IAMReadOnlyAccess) to the agent role, then rerun the audit, or do it manually via CLI, or paste the policy for a merge suggestion. Iteration 3 gives no recommendation at all - it simply says the audit is running and will report back, with no call to action or alternative path for the user.

format_consistency.reasoning: Iterations 1 and 2 use similar structured formats with bolded headers and bullet/numbered lists explaining the failure, limits, and next steps. Iteration 3 is a short, single-paragraph prose statement with no sections, headers, or lists, making it structurally distinct from the other two.
